drug_class: Antimalarial / Antiparasitic (also used as a Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug)
purpose: Chloroquine is mainly used to prevent and treat malaria, a serious infection spread by mosquito bites. It is also sometimes used to treat certain autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Your doctor may prescribe it for travel to areas where malaria is common or to help control inflammation in your body.
how_it_works: Chloroquine works by getting inside the malaria parasite and disrupting its ability to survive and grow. It interferes with a process the parasite needs to digest your red blood cells, essentially poisoning it from the inside. For autoimmune conditions, it helps calm down an overactive immune system that is mistakenly attacking your own body.
common_side_effects: Upset stomach, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, headache, dizziness, and mild skin itching are the most common side effects. Some people may notice a slight change in skin color or bleaching of their hair with long-term use. Taking it with food can help reduce stomach upset.
warnings: The most serious concern with long-term use is potential damage to your eyes, specifically to the retina, which can affect your vision. You should get regular eye check-ups while on this medication. It can also affect your heart rhythm, so tell your doctor if you have heart problems. Avoid this medication if you have a known allergy to it or related drugs. Do not take more than prescribed — overdose can be very dangerous, even life-threatening.
typical_dosing: For malaria prevention, adults usually take 500 mg once a week, starting 1-2 weeks before travel and continuing for 4 weeks after returning. For treatment of malaria, a higher dose is taken over 3 days as directed by your doctor. For lupus or arthritis, the dose is usually lower and taken daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions exactly.
